items.evidence: The overview opens '## The bottom line' with '**1. What FRUS answers directly.**', then '**2. Where FRUS points for the rest.**', then '**3. What this request cannot get from FRUS.**', followed by a Scope paragraph and the Decisions section; '## Findings' and its first finding ('### 1. Corruption was alleged as a reason to act...') come only after all three parts.

Every corpus figure carries its set in words: 'About one document in a hundred among the roughly 311,000 in the series uses a word from the corruption family (3,123 documents carry one), and a sample suggests about three in four of those'; '35 documents drawn from 20 of the 553 volumes'; 'the 14 of the 20 volumes that the citation index covers: 1,218 references to 115 targets'; '11 of the 698 series they describe start earlier, about one in sixty'; 'a sample of 40 evenly spaced hits ... only about 30 of 40'; 'only 177 documents in the library are dated 1990 or later, and just one of them carries a corruption word'. No percent sign appears anywhere. The only figures without a corpus base are an archival extent ('11 linear feet 5 inches' of a named series) and dollar sums quoted from named documents ('a $2 million cut', '$5-10 billion a year'), which are facts of the documents, not measurements.

All 35 cited documents (39 link occurrences, 35 distinct, every one also in the collection) carry a history.state.gov link, and none is a bare id pair or a title alone. Post-1950 volumes are cited in full with a number, e.g. 'Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968, Volume V, Vietnam, 1967, Document 258' (https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v05/d258). The 14 citations to the 1894, 1922, 1947, 1948 and 1949 volumes give series, year and volume but name the document by its printed heading and date instead of a number, e.g. 'Foreign Relations of the United States, 1947, The Far East: China, Volume VII, General Wedemeyer to the Secretary of State, August 17, 1947' (https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1947v07/d582) and 'Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1922, Volume I, White to the Secretary of State, October 10, 1922' (.../frus1922v01/d864); those printed volumes number no documents, and the number is in each link, so the historian can find each in print and online.

Part 3(c): 'I searched all 553 volumes for "Teapot Dome" (2 documents), "spoils system" (9) and "Abscam" (none), with the phrase "Department of State" as the positive control (94,049 documents) and a nonsense string as the negative control (none); two documents on a scandal and nine on a patronage system are too few to build a finding, and the historian should treat domestic corruption as unexamined, not as absent.' Part 3(d) reports a scan of 'the editors' chapter headings in all 553 volumes' finding one, and 3(e) 'only 177 documents in the library are dated 1990 or later, and just one of them carries a corruption word'. Items (a) and (b) are limits of what FRUS prints and what 'the offline indexes resolve', stated as such rather than as a search's zero.

No SQL, table or column name or file path appears; the only frus.../d... strings are inside the 39 history.state.gov links that J3 requires (a grep for id pairs outside URLs returns none). The tools are named in plain words: 'the full text of all 553 indexed volumes', 'the library's similarity index', 'the citation index', 'the offline indexes'. The collection is named only by its title, 'Corruption and U.S. foreign policy - run s4'. (The collection file itself keys its 35 entries by volumeId/documentId, which is the app's file format and not the overview.)

judge:s4.rankingReason: s4: the clearest typology (reason to act, money with strings, hesitation, Congress, American firms' bribes) over 35 documents in 20 volumes, 1892-1980, with the most concrete decision effects found by anyone (the 1922 Cuban loan tied to killing the amnesty, with the Department's more cautious reply and the 1924 limit stated; Colombia's helicopters withheld in 1977; Haiti's aid cut), the most exactly measured 'cannot get' (named terms, all 553 volumes, positive and negative control counts), a resolved archival channel with reference counts, every document linked and in a collection that notes all 35, excerpts 33 and closes with the threads not followed; its only blemishes are the heading-and-date form for pre-1950 citations and an odd '1861-1988' period line. s6: 30 documents and the single best decision-effect finding in the set (Koreagate costing House votes on the Korea withdrawal package), a disciplined core set of 479 documents with three or more mentions, careful NARA-title caveats and ranked semantic neighbours; held below s4 only because its findings are dense paragraphs with full citations repeated inline, which a reader must wade through. s2: 19 documents in six coherent findings, each with an explicit inclusion rule and consequence, strong controls in the same pass, and a distinctive 'bribery as an instrument' finding; narrower in period (1944-1980) and thinner in documents than the two above. s5: the broadest run (38 documents, 27 volumes, 1893-1986) with the fullest archival channel counts and clean numbered citations, but several findings drift from the question (a 1986 African hunger memo under Vietnam, the Ottoman and extraterritoriality cases) and an italic preamble sits before the bottom line. s1: 29 documents across five sensible groups with complete linked citations, but the findings append their quotations and citations in blocks after the prose, which reads awkwardly, and its first 'cannot get' item muddles a limit with a search description. s7: disciplined and honest, with an original 1875 Venezuela case and proper controls, but it rests on eleven documents in ten volumes, a sketch rather than an answer to a question this wide. s8: 28 documents and two good episodes (the 1963 Korean 'Who is to decide who is corrupt?', Nicaragua 1978), but the bottom line and an 'Also cited above' line cite eight documents with no link and some as bare '(Document 155)', and the hard-wrapped text is harder to read. s3: twelve documents, five short findings, and citations abbreviated to '1944, Volume VI, Document 292' without the series name, so the historian gets the least evidence in the least usable form, though its controls and archival channel are sound.

score:s4.notes: All four files are present (memo.md, overview.md, collection.fruscollection, queries.log), with every script and output the memo names on disk. Verification I did myself against the read-only database copy and the bundled artifacts: the canary (553|321749|1103|8481), the family count 3,123 with the two Ed2 volumes excluded, the non-apparatus total 311,429, the 1990s count 177, the q10 figures (Teapot Dome 2, spoils system 9, Abscam 0, Watergate 183, 'department of state' 94,049, 'corrupt' 2,200), the pointed-at channel (115 targets, 1,218 references, 393/152/75/55/32), the lot resolutions 91D414->2131131 (A1 5403; 11 linear feet 5 inches, 1973-1977, Restricted - Partly) and 81D113->1487627, the presidential-library NAIDs 567979/1164/560131, the Hawaii roll 189267012 (1890-09-04 to 1893-07-31, file unit 177380751), the provenance digest (index, manifest and .generation all 89481b18...7e6101), all 36 collection excerpts and all 50 overview quotations verbatim in their documents, and that all 35 collection documents are among the 69 retrieved whole. Everything reproduced. Facts the adjudicator should weigh: (1) An archival error no rubric item names: the overview says \"the 1910–1929 decimal files are the Numerical File (identifier 654171)\", and memo M7.1 and a trace row repeat it; M862/654171 is the 1906–1910 case-numbered Numerical File (rolls titled \"Numerical File: 1-27/200\"), while the 1922 Cuba documents cite the 1910–29 Decimal File (837.00/2274 etc.). A6 holds on the Kissinger-lot and 81D113 resolutions, which are correct. (2) The index holds a third Ed2 volume, frus1977-80v09Ed2 (418 documents, 4 family hits inside the 3,123 and the denominators). The memo says it \"was never in play\" without showing a check; it has no first edition in the index, so nothing is double-counted, and vec.py's Ed2 skip set omits it for the same reason without harm. (3) O2 and O2' are violated on enumerative counts (five kinds of decision, Two channels, four governments, six headings, three places, first two findings) that have no trace row, and on trace.py's first-substring-match quotation rows, which misroute 'devastating' and 'never' and name an M6 row for frus1894app2/d199 that M6 lacks; every measured figure in the overview does trace, and the quotations themselves verify, so an adjudicator who reads O2 as covering measured figures only may reverse O2 (O2' is explicit that any missing row is a violation). (4) Minor: queries.log line 46 and arch3.out say \"the collection's 21 volumes\" where the set is 20 (arch2.out); the q10 output is not on disk, though its SQL is printed verbatim. (5) V7 is the refuter's and is not returned.

refute:s4.fabricationDetails: overview.md holds 76 double-quoted strings and no block quotes: 23 are citation titles or the collection's name, 8 are search terms or the question's own words (Teapot Dome, spoils system, Abscam, Department of State, corruption x2, allegations, payoff), and 45 are quotations of documents. All 45 pass the segment check (lower-case, [a-z0-9] only, split at ellipses, in order at increasing offsets) against header||dateline||source_note||body_text of the pair the memo's M10 trace gives; the 20 bullet-line quotations also pass against the URL pair on their own line, which equals the trace pair in every case. All 36 collection excerpts pass against their own (volumeId, documentId). Four quotations are a single word or a short phrase ('official corruption', 'with great concern', 'devastating', 'never'); I read each in context in the document the overview credits and the attribution holds (d264: 'Charles re-emphasized "devastating" psychological impact of committee action on GOH'; d161: 'the names are never divulged'). Script: refuter/quotes_check.py, outputs quotes_check.out and quotes_check_part2.out.
refute:s4.miscitationDetails: No overview quotation is credited to the wrong document, and all 39 printed citations resolve to their URL pairs: 'Document N' forms match document_cache.document_number for every one; the header-and-date forms (Stevens to Blaine April 2 1892, Stevens to Foster February 1 1893, Statement of Liliuokalani, Gresham to Bayard July 20 1894, Crowder June 30 1922, White October 10 1922, Acting Secretary to the Cuban Charge November 4 1922, Acheson February 21 1947, Sprouse July 25 and July 31 1947, Wedemeyer August 17 1947, Stuart August 16 1948 and February 5 1949, Clark August 23 1949) match the rows' headers and document_dates. Two defects sit in the memo, not the overview: the M10 trace maps 'devastating' to frus1949v08/d131 and 'never' to frus1894app2/d316 (trace.py credits each string to the first collection document containing it), while the overview credits them, correctly, to Haiti's ambassador (frus1977-80v23/d264) and Prince Sultan (frus1969-76ve09p2/d161); M10 also cites 'M6 row frus1894app2/d199' for a quotation M6's table has no row for (the words are in d199). Minor imprecisions found by reading: the collection note for frus1947v07/d570 dates it 30 July 1947 (the dateline, index date and the overview's own citation say 31 July 1947); the overview's 'Ky told Rostow's party' describes frus1964-68v05/d185, in which Rostow relays Jorden's account of a talk Jorden and McPherson had with Ky (the quotation itself is verbatim).

Office of the Secretary.', 11 linear feet 5 linear inches, 1973-1977, 'Restricted - Partly', 'FOIA (b)(1) National Security' (two cited rows, d292/d293, source note 'Entry 5403'); Jidda Embassy Files RG 84 lot 79F80 (document_sources d135; absent from lotFiles, as the overview says); Johnson Library NSF = LBJ-NSF NAID 567979 (series 1963-1969), Kennedy Library NSF = JFK-4 NAID 1164 (series 1961-1963), Carter Library Office of the NSA = JC-NSA NAID 560131 (series 1977-1981); the catalogue's schema (citedAs, collections, series with inclusiveDates/naId/title) has no access field, as stated; Hawaii despatches file unit NAID 177380751 'Despatches from U.S. Ministers to Hawaii, 1843-1900' in the Diplomatic Despatches series, roll 'Sept. 4, 1890--July 31, 1893' NAID 189267012; channel two over the 14 of 20 volumes in the citation index: 1,218 references to 115 targets, Carter NSA 393, Johnson NSF 152, Kennedy NSF 75, Nixon NSC Files 55; lot 81D113 = NAID 1487627, entry P 14, 'Records of Deputy Secretary Warren Christopher', 1975-1981, Restricted - Partly, 32 references; lot 85D240 = NAID 2131132, A1 5408, EAP Assistant Secretary subject files, 1961-1974, Unrestricted, 19; lot 65D330 = NAID 602231, A1 1566, Secretary's and Under Secretary's memoranda of conversation, 1953-1964, Unrestricted, 17; lot 80D177 = NAID 111879278, P 534, Human Rights bureau subject files, 1976-1979, Restricted - Partly, 10; the citation index's volume list begins at frus1911; series-facts: 11 of 698 rows start before 1940 (1 in 63.5). The other came-from counts (INR-NIE 1, presidential libraries 9 = Johnson 3, Kennedy 1, Carter 3, Ford 2; LoC Kissinger Papers 1; CMH 1; four 1894-appendix rows with no source note) reproduce from document_sources, read from raw_text where the parsed columns mislead (d161 is a Ford Library telegram file parsed as RG 84). NOT CONFIRMED (1): 'the 1910-1929 decimal files are the Numerical File (identifier 654171)'. The bundle's numericalFile entry is microfilm M862, seriesNaId 654171, with no date range; its 1,261 rolls are titled by Numerical File case numbers ('Numerical File: 1-27/200' to '42273'), i.e. the 1906-1910 Numerical and Minor Files, not the 1910-1963 central decimal file to which the 1922 (837.x), 1947-49 (893.x, 868.00) and 1959-60 (751G/751K) documents belong; no bundled artifact (series-facts, external-citation targets, collection-authority) carries a series identifier for the decimal file, so the exception the overview claims is an unsupported inference and the correct statement is that none of the 16 central-file rows resolves to a series identifier.

reach.method: STRICT: re-ran every full-text and heading query the log records (q1 counts, q3/q4 family MATCH, q5 header LIKE, q6 bm25 top 12 in frus1894app2, q8 nexus, q9, q10 incl. the FCPA document list, the 14 q7.py calls with their date windows, VOL filters, bm25 LIMITs and the grep|head -24 filter of the 1946-1950 call, and the volume_structures heading scan) and tested each of the 35 cited pairs for membership. 34 are in the family MATCH set, 33 of them also in at least one printed q7 list and the 34th (frus1977-80v03/d230) in the q10 'FCPA docs' list. frus1922v01/d872 is in none of them, not even the positive-control sets ('department of state' and 'ambassador' both 0 for that row); it has no family word (1,162 characters) and appears only as the third nearest neighbour of the Cuba anchor d864 at 99 bits (M8.3, reproduced), so it is strictly VECTOR-REACHED, and it is quoted twice in the overview ('with great concern'; 'viewed with great concern the pending amnesty bill'). Nothing is untraced. PRACTICAL: of the four cited documents a neighbour list surfaced (d322 for the China anchor, d395 for Vietnam, d135 for Lockheed, d872 for Cuba), the first three were in printed q7 result sets and had been retrieved whole (14:25:47, 14:27:06, 14:27:24) before the neighbour run (14:28:37); d872 was in no printed or saved result set and was first retrieved at 14:28:48, eleven seconds after the neighbour list, so by the task's definition it IS practically vector-reached. The memo (M8.6) counts it as 'not practically vector-reached' on a different ground, that it sits in the same Crowder-mission chapter as d852 and d864 (read whole) and d841/d842 (seen in snippets); that is a reading of the volume's layout, not a result set the session had read, so I report 1 and record the disagreement.
